You're right, and my earlier answer was wrong. The fork stopped being a build input on 2026-08-13. I had inferred the deploy source from the template repo's committed Dockerfile without checking whether that was what production actually ran.

**What happened on 08-13.** A Codex session found the Railway rebuild failing on the fork's pinned commit. It ran `railway down` on both environments, cloned the template repo into a scratch folder, rewrote the Dockerfile there to install OpenClaw, the Codex plugin and the Discord plugin from the npm registry at pinned versions, and deployed that with `railway up`. It then deleted the codex-realtime-dev environment. Production has run that npm-based image since, at version 2026.7.1-2, with no fork code in it. That is also the normal way to do this. The upstream template installs from a release tag, and the 29-patch fork branch only ever existed for the voice experiment.

**The bold.org commit.** You made it on 2026-02-26 and it adds one file, `assets/bold-profile.png`, to the fork's main. That branch is otherwise identical to upstream as of 2026-02-18 and is now about 74,000 commits behind. It looks like the repo was used once as an image host. It has nothing to do with deployment.

**What still points at the fork:**
- The template repo's committed main still has the old Dockerfile that fetches from the fork. The npm-based Dockerfile that production actually runs exists only as an uncommitted diff in a Codex scratch folder under your Documents. If Railway is still connected to the GitHub repo, any push to main would rebuild from the fork and fail. I can't confirm the connection state because the Railway CLI token has expired.
- The open upstream PR [openclaw/openclaw#119001](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/119001) has its head on the fork. Deleting the fork closes it permanently.

**So, can you delete it?** Yes, once the template repo is fixed. The order that avoids surprises:

1. Commit the recovery Dockerfile and entrypoint from the scratch checkout to the template repo's main, so the committed source matches production and no longer references the fork. I can do this if you want, but it's a push to a public repo so I won't without a go-ahead.
2. Delete the fork from GitHub. Accept that the PR closes.
3. Optionally run `railway login` so I can confirm the service's source settings and check what the mobot project builds from. It has no deployment records on the template repo, so it isn't built from there through the GitHub integration.

**No, don't delete it.** Your Railway bots are built from that fork, and an open upstream pull request lives on it.

**Why it exists.** The fork was created on 2026-02-18, but the work that matters was pushed in August. Branch `deploy/stable-2026.7.1-2` is upstream's v2026.7.1-2 release plus 29 fork-only commits that backport native Discord realtime voice into the stable line. Branch `agent/codex-native-realtime-voice` is the head of your open PR [openclaw/openclaw#119001](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/119001), last updated 2026-08-30. The hundreds of other branches are just upstream's branches copied at fork time. It is public because GitHub does not allow a fork of a public repo to be private.

**What breaks if you delete it:**
- The Railway template repo's Dockerfile fetches OpenClaw source from the fork at a pinned commit, which is the tip of the stable-voice branch and does not exist on upstream main. The live bots would keep running because the package sits on the `/data` volume, but the next Railway build would fail at the git fetch step.
- GitHub closes the upstream PR when its head fork is deleted, and it cannot be reopened from a non-fork copy.

**When it becomes safe.** Point the Dockerfile at a different source and either get the PR merged or abandon it. If upstream merges the voice work and you move to a release that includes it, the fork has no remaining purpose.
